Chapter 3: The Power of the Erotic—Reclaiming Joy and Connection
Have you ever noticed a current of energy humming quietly beneath the surface of everyday life? It’s something deeper than just routine or habit—almost like a well of feeling, creativity, and connection that we rarely talk about. Most people think of the erotic as something strictly sexual, but what if I told you it’s so much more than that?
The erotic, in its richest sense, is really a wellspring of joy, inspiration, and self-knowledge. It’s this force that can transform not just your own experience, but the way you relate to others, too.
Picture this: a painter completely absorbed in color and movement, not thinking, just feeling. Or a dancer who gets lost in the music, every step guided by something deeper than thought. Maybe it’s a cook, breathing in the aroma of a simmering stew, hands moving by instinct. In these moments, being alive feels almost magical. The line between you and the world gets fuzzy, and a real sense of satisfaction takes root.
That’s the erotic at work—when you embrace your own desires, feelings, and passions, you tap into a powerful kind of energy.
For folks whose identities have been pushed to the margins, reclaiming this energy isn’t just empowering—it’s essential. We live in a world that tells us to distrust our bodies, hide our feelings, and always put logic first. But choosing to honor the erotic is almost an act of rebellion. It’s like saying, “My joy matters. My pleasure isn’t a selfish extra. It’s something I need.”
And when you think about it, this isn’t just about feeling good for yourself. It’s a political statement—a way to push back against a society that wants to box you in.
Let me share a story. There’s a woman who, after years of always putting others first, finally decides to do something for herself. She starts taking long walks, listens to music that moves her, and reconnects with friends she’s missed. At first, she feels guilty—she’s been taught that self-care is selfish, that her value is measured by how much she sacrifices. But as she starts leaning into those moments of joy, something shifts. She actually feels stronger. The more she cares for herself, the more she has to give to others. Her relationships grow deeper, her work becomes more meaningful, and suddenly, the world doesn’t seem quite so harsh.
This isn’t just about individual happiness, either. When we embrace the erotic together, it becomes a source of solidarity and resistance. Think about gatherings where people feel safe to really be themselves—to share their dreams and fears without judgment. In those spaces, something powerful happens. The walls built by things like race, gender, sexuality, or class start to soften. People connect not by pretending their differences don’t exist, but by honoring every part of what it means to be human.
Here’s something to pay attention to: Most of us have been taught to fear our own feelings. The world encourages us to numb out, distract ourselves, and fit in—so much so that we forget what real joy feels like. But when you tap into the erotic, you remember what it means to feel truly alive. This energy is what fuels creativity, keeps activists going, and helps us imagine a world that’s more just, caring, and alive.
Reclaiming the erotic isn’t a one-and-done thing. It’s a practice—something you come back to again and again. It takes courage and patience, and you’ll need to challenge a lifetime of messages about what you should or shouldn’t feel. But the rewards? They’re huge. You’ll discover a deeper sense of self, build richer relationships, and find a renewed commitment to creating a world where everyone has a chance to thrive.
